messages.subject: 2 sided estimate
messages.body_plain:
I am analyzing a survey in which I want to do a separate estimate for
each side of the survey platform. The two estimates will then be
summed to get the total estimate. However, are the variances of the
two estimates additive as well or is there a dependence issue here?

Thanks,

Daniel Pike.

messages.subject: Re: 2 sided estimate
messages.body_plain:
Err... it's not as easy as that I'm afraid.  Distance does
post-stratification before sending the data off to the analysis engines.
  So, the analysis engine would see two strata (left and right), with
lines within each strata, and it would bootstrap the lines within strata
independently, which is not what is wanted here.  I'm afraid the only
way I know of to take account of the dependence is to program a
bootstrap outside of the Distance interface - something about which
there are several postings already on the list.  On the plus side,
ignoring the dependence will result in an overestimate of variance, and
an overestimate is better than an underestimate...

I wonder why one would want a separate estimate for each side of a
survey platform in the first place.  If it's to account for observer
differences in detection prob, one can do this by having observer or
side as covariates in the mcds or mrds analysis engines. I expect I'm
missing something obvious here...

  - Len Thomas

messages.subject: Re: 2 sided estimate
messages.body_plain:
Hi

The basic issue is that we have 2 platforms on one side and one on the
other. I can do MRDS analysis on one side only to get p(0) values for
the primary, secondary and combined platforms. My idea was to use the
MRDS estimate for the side with 2 platforms, and apply the p(0) for
the primary platform to the estimate from the side with one observer,
then sum the estimates. However I am not clear about variance
estimation in this case.

Another way would be to just "pretend" there is a secondary platform
on both sides and just have no sightings for the secondary on the side
where there is no observer. The overall p(0) values for the primary,
secondary and combined platforms would then be correct, but the p(0)
values for the secondary and combined platforms would be lower,
reflecting the fact that there are fewer sightings on the side with
one observer only. I guess variance estimation is more straightforward
in this case.

Thanks for your help,

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Daniel-

I've not tried it but one thought would be to add the dummy data for the
missing observer and including a covariate that is 0 except for the
dummy observer and then using that covariate in the mark-recapture
model.  It should go to a large negative number on the logit scale
(p=0).  Also, you would want to look at a side (left/right) effect for
the distance model for the scale parameter.  This will get around your
original issue.

--jeff

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alex, list,

Yes, in Distance 6.0 you can use the new systematic design variance
estimators of Fewster et al. (2009) in addition to having a single level
of stratification.  These estimators give a much better estimate of true
variance for systematic parallel line transect designs, and as a bonus
the estimate should be much lower if there are strong spatial trends in
density running perpendicular to the lines.

To set the variance estimator, choose the Advanced... button in the
Variance tab of the model definition (assuming you're using CDS or MCDS;
for MRDS the new systematic variance estimators are available in R, but
this is not yet exposed in the interface).  Fewster recommends the
overlapping strata estimator (O2) over the non-overlapping on (S2) - see
the paper for details.  Note that it is incorrect to try both and choose
the one with the smaller variance estimate!

You didn't say, but I assume you have a systematic parallel line
transect design -- this is the situation the estimators were designed for.

You can specify analysis options for the SpeciesMonth stratum as usual -
nothing is changed there.

Note that it would be incorrect to post-stratify into "good" and and
"poor" end having seen the data and realized that species density is
higher at one end than the other: such things should be decided at the
design stage, not after peeking at the data to reveal density patterns.
  If you do it at after looking at the data, you can get a badly
underestimated variance.  However, you don't need to do this in any case.

Cheers,

  - Len Thomas

Fewster, R.M., S.T. Buckland, K.P. Burnham, D.L. Borchers, P.E. Jupp,
J.L. Laake and L. Thomas. 2009. Estimating the encounter rate variance
in distance sampling. Biometrics 65: 225-236.
Copy available at
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/papers/FewsterBiometrics2009.pdf

Hi Alex.  You don't clarify what your existing strata are.  If your
design has one set of equally-spaced lines throughout your study area,
then you can ignore existing strata, and pair up lines to get a better
estimate of the systematic variance.  If you have different sampling
intensities in each stratum, and sufficient lines per stratum, you could
apply the technique within strata.  However, I suspect even there, you
would get a pretty good (better?) estimate if you ignore strata, and
just pair up neighbouring lines throughout the study region.

Incidentally, our paper on getting better estimates of systematic
variances has now appeared:

Fewster, R.M., Buckland, S.T., Burnham, K.P., Borchers, D.L., Jupp,
P.E., Laake, J.L. and Thomas, L. 2009.  Estimating the encounter rate
variance in distance sampling.  /Biometrics/ *65*, 225-236.

design has one set of equally-spaced lines throughout your study area,

estimate of the systematic variance.  If you have different sampling
intensities in each stratum, and sufficient lines per stratum, you could
apply the technique within strata.  However, I suspect even there, you
would get a pretty good (better?) estimate if you ignore strata, and
just pair up neighbouring lines throughout the study region.

I am having difficulty determining the mean density for Tasmanian pademelon (Thylogale billardierii) pooled over four line transect surveys undertaken a month apart. Sample sizes for individual sightings were small so I have manually pooled the data (total n = 60) and analysed through the DISTANCE program using Conventional Distance Sampling Analysis (self-taught!).

 # samples     :    16

  Parameter   Estimate       Error      of Variation     Confidence Interval

    D        0.71910      0.57635          80.15      0.16069       3.2181
    N         1213.0       972.20          80.15       271.00       5429.0
  ---------  -----------  -----------  --------------  ----------------------

Detection probability
                        Estimate      %CV     df     95% Confidence Interval
                        ------------------------------------------------------
 Half-normal/Cosine
                 m       2.0000

                 AIC     429.65
                 AICc    429.86
                 BIC     433.80

                 ESW     19.495        8.34    57.00  16.500       23.034

Janeane Ingram

messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

We have some questions regarding structuring and analyzing distance
sampling data for an ongoing study of wintering grassland birds.  The
study design is as follows.  There are 10 study areas (Grassland
Priority Conservation Areas, or GPCAs) that are widely distributed
inside the study region, which is roughly 1000 x 400 km.  Within each of
these GPCAs are a grid of blocks, roughly 18 x 18 km in size.  Blocks
were chosen at random within each GPCA and in proportion to the total
number available within each GPCA.  Within each block, three random
points along roads were selected.  From these three points, two opposing
1 km line-transects were run, perpendicular to the road, by separate
observers.  We have three years of data.

Strata are organized as follows:

Region
    GPCA
       Block - contains area values
          Sample - contains transect names and a field "Block-Year" for
post-stratification purposes
             Observation

We want to estimate bird density for each GPCA for each of the three
years of the study.  In addition, we would like each stratum estimate
for GPCA-Year to be the mean of block density estimates weighted by the
grassland area within each block.  We would also like to make use of all
observations from all years for the creation of detection functions.
This allows us a large enough sample size to create a detection function
for several rare and threatened species.  Our understanding is that
Distance only uses weighting to combine strata level into a global
density estimate.  However, we would like strata level (GPCA) density
estimates that are weighted by grassland area in the blocks. We plan to
use block level density estimates in the SPsurvey package in R
(total.est function) and/or the delta method to calculate weighted GPCA
estimates by year (and associated variances) using the mean of block
estimates weighted by the grassland area within each block.  Block
estimates are derived by post-stratifying on a field in the sample layer
that is a combination of Block ID and Year.

The main thought behind doing this that it seems logical that densities
in blocks with more grassland should be given more weight towards a GPCA
average (although there is some uncertainty among staff that this is the
correct course of action).  We were also hoping to avoid the use of
multipliers given that we are estimating densities for ~30 species.

1. Is calculating the weighted stratum level estimates outside Distance
our only course of action?
2. Considering the blocks were randomly selected within the GPCAs, is it
necessary to weight the GPCA density estimates by the area of grassland
in the blocks?
3. If the blocks were not selected randomly or were systematically
surveyed, would it then be advisable to weight GPCA density estimates by
the area of grassland in the blocks?

Any help is much appreciated,
Greg

ur comment=2C "If the blocks were not selected randomly or were systematica=
lly surveyed=2C would it then be advisable to weight GPCA density estimates=

verage probability (i.e.=2C how to weight survey blocks)=2C and are particu=
larly interested in the role of an environmental covariate=2C then this str=
ikes me as a problem that lends itself inherently to density surface modell=
ing.  These methods relax the assumptions about representative coverage=2C =
and just require you to have reasonable coverage across the range of covari=
ates (spatial and environmental=2C in this case).  In Arvind's update=2C th=
e goals you both outline ("to estimate the population size of each species =
in each GPCA in each year. Because grassland area in each survey block vari=
es=2C but survey effort is generally the same") describe a spatio-temporal =
model to me.  The DSM help files in D6 have good examples.  You can easily =
use year as a covariate (factor) and estimate abundance in any sub-area.
=20
If you're married to a conventional distance sampling analysis=2C it seems =
to me that you want to weight strata according to coverage probability=2C n=
ot by some environmental covariate that you chose post-hoc:  you didn't inc=
lude it at the design stage.  Or am I misunderstanding?  Did you choose you=
r blocks based on % grassland cover?  Given the situation you describe=2C a=
 conventional method could be used to test whether density is indeed higher=

iology (some birds prefer grassland) to discuss why density might have been=
 higher in some blocks than others.  But it might be more efficient to do a=
 model-based estimate -- if you want an abundance estimate by location and =
year=2C DSM methods will give you that=2C while modelling the relationship =
between habitat and abundance directly. =20
=20
Good luck.  Sounds as though you have a lot of data to work with and great =
coverage.

messages.subject: Occupancy vs. DS ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a question for you:

Several methods exist to compute detectability, e.g. DS (Distance Sampling),
Capture-Mark-Recapture (CMR) and Occupancy (software PRESENCE).

I see a lot of effort re. Occupancy, and which deal mostly just with
presence/absence (I am aware of the new efforts to handle continuous data).

I believe that getting at populations, densities, is a key goal though for
good species management etc.
So I am not so clear really how to go from pres/abs, occupancy, to
densities, e.g. from DS, or to link and assess both.

My real question is about the following:

Occupancy is inherently aspatial, it's usually just a POINT ESTIMATE, and
thus, 1 dimensional (strictly speaking: the tip of a needle). There is no
area for this at all.

In DS, we have AREA included (2 dimensional), and deal with detection width
or detection radius.
We also know that such detection widths are inherently NOT constant, and
ought to be modeled (e.g. declining detection function, dynamic changes).

Assigning 'just an area estimate' to a sighting is a rather critical factor
for any valid density estimation, right ?

So how can Occupancy and DS truly be compared ?
And if it cannot, what does that mean ?

I see applications where Occupancies get obtained for areas (e.g. plots,
squares), but how can that really be valid for true density estimates ?
Doesn't DS teach us otherwise: Any centimeter counts, not ?
(try it out with your own data and when you start to extrapolate to larger
areas and landscapes)

Isn't the same problem true for CMR as well ?

I would welcome any thoughts and ideas about this.

Thanks in advance; very best

    F.

messages.subject: Re: Occupancy vs. DS ?
messages.body_plain:
Occupancy simply converts abundance to 0/1 and can be defined for an
area although I'm not sure it always is in applications.  It uses
multiple visits or multiple methods with some fairly strong assumptions
to assess detection probability.  Usually requires 5-6 visits.  I can
see it working well for relatively sedentary critters like amphibians,
or territorial birds and with well-defined or possibly discrete sites
(e.g, ponds).

--jeff
